scenes.say: Flip a switch and the light comes on, instantly. But the electricity lighting your room was made only a fraction of a second ago, maybe hundreds of kilometres away. Let's follow it home.
scenes.title: How electricity *gets home*
scenes.subtitle: From the power station to your wall socket

scenes.say: The first thing to know is that the grid has almost no storage. Every moment, power stations must produce exactly as much electricity as everyone is using.
Most electricity starts with something spinning. Steam from burning gas or coal can spin a turbine. So can water falling through a dam, or wind pushing on giant blades.
scenes.heading: Something spins

scenes.say: Solar panels are the exception. They turn light straight into electricity, with no moving parts at all.
Inside a generator, the spinning shaft turns magnets past coils of copper wire. A moving magnetic field pushes electrons along the wire, and that push is electricity.
scenes.heading: Inside a generator

scenes.say: In most of Europe and Asia, generators spin in step with the grid, flipping the current back and forth fifty times every second.
scenes.label: times per second the current reverses

scenes.say: Why does the current flip back and forth at all? In the eighteen eighties, Thomas Edison championed direct current, while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse backed alternating current.
scenes.heading: The current war

scenes.say: Alternating current won, mostly because its voltage is easy to change with a transformer. That one advantage shaped every grid on the planet.
scenes.text: AC won because voltage is *easy to change*

scenes.say: Here is a problem. Sending power over long wires wastes energy as heat, and the higher the current, the bigger the loss. So engineers trade current for voltage.
scenes.heading: The long-distance problem

scenes.say: A transformer at the power station steps the voltage up, often to hundreds of thousands of volts, before the power leaves on the tall transmission towers.
scenes.heading: Step up

scenes.say: Some long-distance lines carry four hundred thousand volts, enough that the air near the wires can crackle and hum.
scenes.label: volts on long-distance lines

scenes.say: Those lines connect power stations across whole countries into one giant network called the grid. If one station trips offline, others pick up the slack.
Because supply and demand must match, the grid's frequency is a live health signal. If demand outruns supply, the generators slow down very slightly, and the frequency starts to fall.
Operators respond in layers. Spinning generators resist the change for a few seconds, automatic reserves kick in within seconds, and slower plants are started over the next few minutes.
scenes.heading: Keeping the pulse steady

scenes.say: When those layers fail, you get a blackout. Large blackouts are rare, but they show how tightly connected the whole system is.
Grid operators watch the network around the clock. They forecast demand, schedule which plants run, and react within seconds when something changes.
scenes.heading: Grid operators

scenes.say: Demand has a daily rhythm. It rises when people wake up, dips in the afternoon, and peaks in the evening when everyone gets home and starts cooking.
Near towns, the power reaches a substation. Transformers there step the voltage down, and smaller distribution lines carry it along the streets.
scenes.heading: Step down

scenes.say: Even with high voltage, some energy is lost on the way. In many grids, around five to eight percent of electricity disappears as heat in wires and transformers.
scenes.label: lost as heat on the way

scenes.say: One last transformer, often a grey can on a pole or a green box on the pavement, lowers the voltage again to what your home can safely use.
scenes.text: The last step: *a box on your street*

scenes.say: In many countries that is around two hundred and thirty volts. In North America it is about one hundred and twenty.
scenes.label: at the socket in many countries

scenes.say: At your home, the power passes a meter that records how much you use, then a panel of breakers. Each breaker protects one circuit and cuts the power if too much current flows.
scenes.heading: Inside your home

scenes.say: Many homes now have smart meters. They send readings automatically, can show your use hour by hour, and help the grid plan for busy times.
scenes.heading: Smart meters

scenes.say: And a quick safety reminder. Never touch fallen power lines, and keep water away from sockets. The same push that lights your room can be dangerous.
And here is something surprising. The electrons themselves barely move. They drift along the wire slower than a snail. What travels fast is the push, the energy passed from one electron to the next.
Renewables are changing the grid. Sun and wind cannot be switched on when needed, so grids are adding batteries and smarter controls to store power and balance it.
scenes.heading: A changing grid

scenes.say: Grid-scale battery storage has grown more than tenfold in just a few years.
scenes.label: growth in grid batteries in a few years

scenes.say: Pumped hydro is the oldest big battery. When power is cheap, water is pumped uphill into a reservoir. When demand peaks, it flows back down through turbines.
scenes.heading: The oldest big battery

scenes.say: Pumped hydro and big batteries give back around eighty to ninety percent of the energy put into them.
scenes.label: of stored energy comes back

scenes.say: Some grids now pay people to use less power at peak times, which is often cheaper than building a new power station.
scenes.text: Using less can be *cheaper* than building more

scenes.say: Electric cars could help too. Parked and plugged in, millions of car batteries could charge when power is cheap and give some back when it is scarce.
scenes.heading: Cars as a battery

scenes.say: Long distance links are changing as well. New high voltage direct current lines carry power between countries with less loss than alternating current.
scenes.text: Direct current is *back* for long links

scenes.say: At home, the biggest users are usually heating, cooling, water heaters and old fridges. Small changes there save far more than unplugging a phone charger.
scenes.heading: Where your power goes

scenes.say: So, the whole journey. Something spins or the sun shines. Transformers step the voltage up for the long trip. Substations and street boxes step it back down. And your breakers keep it safe.
scenes.heading: The whole journey

scenes.say: All of that happens in the instant between flipping the switch and the light coming on.
Thanks for following the electricity home. If you learned something, share this with a friend.
scenes.title: Power, explained
